## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

The *Wénshū wèn jīng zìmǔ pǐn dì shísì* (T469) is a one-fascicle alternate translation of chapter 14 of [KR6i0069](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6i/KR6i0069) (T468, Saṅghapāla's *Wénshū wèn jīng*) by the Tang esoteric master Amoghavajra 不空 ([不空](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%B8%8D%E7%A9%BA); 705–774 CE). The Taishō header explicitly cross-references No. 468(14). The chapter concerns the *zìmǔ* 字母 — the Sanskrit alphabet (*akṣaramātṛkā*) — which by Amoghavajra's time had become a central tool of esoteric (*mìjiào* 密教) practice. The text is essentially a translation/retranslation focused on the dhāraṇī function of the Sanskrit syllabary.

**Abstract**

Amoghavajra's translation of the *zìmǔ* chapter as an independent text reflects the central role of the Sanskrit alphabet in esoteric Buddhist practice. The *akṣaramātṛkā* — the 50 (or 42, or 51) Sanskrit syllables — was understood in Tantric Buddhism as the matrix from which all dhāraṇī, mantras, and *bīja* (seed-syllable) meditations are derived. The doctrinal claim that "all dharmas enter into the syllables" provides the metaphysical justification for syllable-based contemplation.

Amoghavajra (705–774 CE) was the third of the famous "Three Great Esoteric Masters" of the Tang (*kāiyuán sān dà shì* 開元三大士) — [善無畏](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%96%84%E7%84%A1%E7%95%8F) Shàn Wúwèi (Śubhākarasiṃha), [金剛智](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%87%91%E5%89%9B%E6%99%BA) Jīngāngzhì (Vajrabodhi), and [不空](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%B8%8D%E7%A9%BA) Bùkōng (Amoghavajra). He inherited Vajrabodhi's lineage, returned to India and Central Asia in 741 CE, and brought back numerous esoteric texts which he translated under imperial patronage. The bulk of his translation work is dated 746–774 CE; this particular text falls within that bracket.
